list.listitem: Treat suspected pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) empirically pending the results of cultures. C
Treat PID based on Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommendations. Parenteral and oral regimens have similar efficacies. Thus most patients can be treated as outpatients. A

Recommended outpatient regimen is ceftriaxone 500 mg IM single dose AND doxycycline 100 mg orally twice a day for 14 days WITH metronidazole 500 mg orally twice a day for 14 days for anaerobic coverage. A
Anaerobic coverage is recommended in all therapeutic regimens. C
Recheck patients after treatment for resolution of symptoms. Patients unresponsive to oral/intramuscular regimens within 72 hours should be considered for IV regimens. C

background.definition: Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) is an inflammatory condition of the female genital tract including any of the following: endometritis, salpingitis, tubo-ovarian abscess, and/or pelvic peritonitis.

list.listitem: More than 1 million women in the United States experience acute PID yearly.
Chlamydial infection rates increased from 251.4 to 539.9/100,000 during the years between 2000 and 2018.
The CDC reports that among women with chlamydial and gonococcal infections, 10% to 20% may develop PID if they do not receive adequate treatment.

In a UK study using data from the National Chlamydia Screening Programme, the risk of PID following an untreated chlamydia infection is 17.1% (95% credible interval [CrI], 6%-29%) and the risk of salpingitis is 7.3% (95% CrI, 2.2%-14.0%). The authors estimated that annual screening in women aged 16 to 24 years would prevent 61% of chlamydia-related PID cases and 22% of all PID cases.
The risk of PID within 90 days following intrauterine device insertion in one population-based study was 0.54% (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.48%-0.60%).

In urban family planning, sexually transmitted disease, and school-based clinics in Baltimore, chlamydia infection was found in 24% of first visits and 14% of repeat visits; 29% of adolescent females had at least one positive test result. Girls who were 14 years old had the highest age-specific prevalence rate (28%).
Based on 2013 data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey, the estimated prevalence of self-reported lifetime PID was 4.4% in sexually-experienced women aged 18 to 44 years.
Lifetime prevalence has decreased steadily since 1995 across all races.
Among women with a prior STI, lifetime prevalence of PID was similar by race (10% vs. 10.3%).

In a Swedish population-based questionnaire study conducted among women giving birth during 1 year, at least one infectious episode was reported by 10.3% of the women and 7.5% had received antibiotics; endometritis was reported by 2.0% of women who received antibiotics and 1.7% who were not given antibiotics.
Annual cost to the US healthcare system is $16.4 billion.

In 2012, the World Health Organization estimated that chlamydial infections, including those resulting in PID, cost 1.43 million disability-adjusted life-years, mostly in low- and middle-income countries.
PID is the most frequent cause of gynecologic emergency room visits.
About 50,000 initial visits for PID occurred in 2014 according to the CDC; rates have steadily decreased since 2005.
More than 100,000 of those infected become infertile. One in 8 women diagnosed with PID will have difficulty with fertility.

Common: Neisseria gonorrhoeae (GC), Chlamydia trachomatis, anaerobes (e.g., Bacteroides fragilis). The CDC notes that the proportion of cases of PID due to GC and chlamydia have decreased to <50%. In a UK study, 35% of cases of PID were caused by chlamydia in women aged 16 to 24 years and 20% in women aged 16 to 44 years.
Uncommon: Gardnerella vaginalis, Haemophilus influenzae, enteric gram negatives, Streptococcus agalactiae, Mycoplasma hominis, Ureaplasma urealyticum.
At one large sexual-health clinic in Australia, no causative organism was identified in more than 60% of PID cases.

The vagina is an environment of fluctuating bacterial flora. In healthy women, lactobacilli dominate, but under varying hormonal influences other naturally-occurring pathogenic bacteria can interrupt the healthy balance, leading to conditions such as bacterial vaginosis.
Menses appears to reduce these cervical defenses.

PID is caused by a breach of the barrier created by the endocervical canal by naturally occurring pathogenic or sexually-transmitted organisms; in the latter case, it is hypothesized that N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis create tubal infection with secondary invasion of other bacteria from the cervix and vagina that ascend into the uterus.
Screen all women 25 years and younger yearly for chlamydia A and gonorrhea. B
Screen all pregnant women for chlamydia and gonorrhea. B
Preoperative prophylactic antibiotics for cesarean delivery decrease the risk of maternal endometritis; consequences for the baby are uncertain.

United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommends screening for GC and chlamydial infections for all sexually-active young women 24 years and younger and for older women who are at risk, regardless of pregnancy status.
The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists recommends screening all pregnant women for syphilis and chlamydia and high-risk pregnant women for gonorrhea.
Six-month screening intervals may be appropriate for higher risk populations.
Offer all patients with PID an HIV test.

Authors of a systematic review found screening women at high risk of chlamydia and female and male high school students reduced the incidence of PID at 1 year; methodologic flaws in the two studies identified could have overestimated the benefits.

A 2014 systematic review for the USPSTF concluded that although screening asymptomatic young women for chlamydia in one good-quality trial did not reduce PID incidence over the subsequent year, chlamydia screening in young women may reduce the incidence based on previous trials.

In an RCT of single episode test and treat versus sample storage and analysis at 1 year (deferred screening) among a group of university women; PID rates were not significantly different between women in the test and treat vs. deferred screening groups at 1 year (1.3% and 1.9%, respectively). Seven of 74 deferred screening women (9.5%) who tested positive for baseline chlamydial infection developed PID over 12 months; however, most episodes of PID occurred in women who tested negative for chlamydia at baseline (79%, 30/38). Twenty-two percent (527/2377) of women reported independent testing for chlamydia during the trial.

A time series analysis for a cohort of 207,695 continuously enrolled privately insured women found increased screening rates associated with decreased PID diagnosis rates 4 months later; for every 10% increase in screening rates there was a 3.6% (chlamydia) and 3.2% (gonorrhea) decrease in the growth rate of the PID diagnosis rate.

Being screened for chlamydia and gonorrhea routinely within 1 year prior to IUD insertion does not reduce the risk of PID. The investigators concluded that testing women based on risk factors on the day of the procedure was the most rational approach.
Based on a Cochrane review, the use of prophylactic antibiotics post IUD insertion does not reduce the risk of PID.

Preoperative prophylactic antibiotics for cesarean delivery decreases the risk of maternal endometritis (RR 0.47; 95% CI, 0.26-0.85) but not neonatal infections or newborn outcomes. This RR is similar to a Cochrane review that found a RR of endometritis with use of prophylactic antibiotics for women undergoing cesarean section of 0.38 (95% CI, 0.34-0.42). Rates of endometritis varied by risk status – for elective procedures, antibiotics reduced endometritis from 39/1000 to 15/1000, and from 160-184/100 to 61-70/1000 in other risk groups.

In a recent RCT of 2013 women undergoing non-elective cesarean delivery, adjunctive azithromycin 500 mg IV in addition to routine antibiotic prophylaxis significantly reduced rates of endometritis (6.1%-3.5% in the intervention group).

Authors of a Cochrane review of 10 high-quality studies found that antibiotic administration preoperatively significantly reduced the risk of composite maternal postpartum infectious morbidity, and specifically reduced postpartum endometritis (RR 0.54; 95% CI, 0.36-0.79), compared to administration after cord clamping. There were no differences in rates of neonatal sepsis.

Based on 7 RCTs, vaginal preparation with povidone-iodine solution immediately before cesarean delivery reduces the risk of postoperative endometritis (8.3% in control groups vs. 4.3% in vaginal cleansing groups; RR 0.45; 95% CI, 0.25-0.81).

The US Preventive Services Task Force (2020) recommends behavioral counseling for all sexually active adolescents and adults who are at increased risk for sexually transmitted infections. While not directly addressed in the evidence summary, this has the potential to reduce PID incidence.
Order a urine pregnancy test for any woman of reproductive age who presents with abdominal pain. C
If increased abdominal or cervical motion tenderness is noted, perform a microscopic analysis of the vaginal discharge and test for chlamydia and gonorrhea. C

Make a presumptive diagnosis of PID if a woman has pelvic or lower abdominal pain; no identified other cause for the illness; amd one of the following: uterine tenderness, adnexal tenderness, or cervical motion tenderness. If PID is suspected, treat. C
A definitive diagnosis can be made on endometrial biopsy, transvaginal ultrasound, or laparoscopy for patients with severe disease or those who fail initial therapy. C

list.listitem: The presentation of PID can range from mild to severe.
Patients can present with lower abdominal pain with/without fever, vaginal discharge (±odor), dyspareunia, or irregular menses.

Historical factors that put women at higher risk include: a positive social history for multiple sexual partners, new sexual partner, unprotected vaginal intercourse, recent IUD insertion, or douching.

The CDC guidelines (2015) recommend that a presumptive diagnosis of PID be made if a woman has pelvic or lower abdominal pain, no identified other cause for the illness, and one of the following: adnexal tenderness, uterine tenderness or cervical motion tenderness. The presence of an oral temperature >101°F, abnormal cervical mucopurulent discharge or cervical friability support the diagnosis.

One history-based prediction model for PID with high specificity included four variables: abnormal vaginal discharge, bilateral pelvic pain, constipation, and presence of an intrauterine device. For ruling out PID, four variables (scattered pain radiation and/or diffuse pain, insidious pain, peritoneal irritation, and abnormal vaginal discharge) were found to identify a low risk group.
The physical examination also varies and can include: cervical discharge, cervical motion tenderness, abdominal tenderness, or a pelvic mass.

In a study of 288 adolescent women who presented to an emergency department with vaginal discharge or lower abdominal pain, the addition of a pelvic exam did not increase sensitivity or specificity for an STI compared with taking a history alone in adolescents at high likelihood (>25%) of having either cervicitis or PID. The addition of the pelvic examination, without urine testing, would have correctly identified an additional 35 women with infection but falsely identified 36 who did not have infection.
Order a urine pregnancy test for any woman of reproductive age who presents with abdominal pain.

If cervical motion tenderness, adnexal mass or tenderness, or abnormal discharge are noted, perform microscopic analysis of the vaginal discharge and obtain laboratory testing for N. gonorrhoeae (culture, nucleic acid amplification test [NAAT], or nucleic acid hybridization test) and C. trachomatis (NAAT).
Gram stain of cervical discharge is very specific for chlamydia infection but lacks sensitivity. Leukocyte esterase is more sensitive but less specific.

An elevated WBC and an elevated ESR or CRP suggest PID including chlamydial PID; the latter can also be used to monitor response to therapy. In a case series of 73 patients with PID, ESR >19.5 mm/1/2 h and CRP >11.5 mg/L were the best predictors of tubo ovarian abscess, which was present in 44 women.

A transvaginal ultrasound is the most sensitive and specific test for PID and can often differentiate between PID and other abdominal etiologies. Ultrasound is also helpful for diagnosing pelvic abscess. However, it is not routinely recommended, as PID is primarily a clinical diagnosis.

Based on a study of 52 patients with clinical suspicion of acute salpingitis of whom 9 were ultimately diagnosed with endometritis and 17 with salpingitis, the presence of bilateral adnexal masses increased the odds of salpingitis by about five fold. Conversely, the absence of bilateral adnexal masses at ultrasound decreased the odds of mild-to-severe acute salpingitis about five fold.
If PID remains highly suspected despite negative clinical tests, a laparoscopy or endometrial biopsy are definitive for the diagnosis of PID.

A presumptive diagnosis of PID can be made if the patient has pelvic or lower abdominal pain; no identified other cause for the illness; and adnexal tenderness, uterine tenderness or cervical motion tenderness. Abnormal vaginal discharge and fever support the diagnosis.
Obtain cultures and begin empiric treatment ().
Pelvic ultrasound can also aid in the diagnosis of PID, especially if other etiologies for the pain are suspected. It may show pelvic abscess or enlargement of pelvic organs.
Treat women who have mild to moderate PID with an outpatient regimen based on 2021 CDC guidelines without risk of long-term sequelae. A
Recommended outpatient regimen is ceftriaxone 500 mg IM single dose AND doxycycline 100 mg orally twice a day for 14 days WITH metronidazole 500 mg orally twice a day for 14 days. A
If there is no improvement with outpatient treatment within 72 hours, admit to the hospital for parenteral treatment. C
If the patient is pregnant, admit for inpatient therapy. C
Outpatient treatment is equivalent to inpatient therapy for most women.

The recommended drug regimens based on 2021 CDC guidelines are shown in . All treatment regimens should cover both N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis. Anaerobic coverage is a must with the diagnosis of a tubo-ovarian abscess; clindamycin is preferred over doxycycline.
In one small RCT, ceftriaxone plus azithromycin (two 1-g doses 1 week apart) was as effective as ceftriaxone and doxycycline (200 mg for 14 days).
Treat inpatients for 48 hours or 24 hours after clinical improvement prior to stopping parenteral treatment and initiating oral treatment.
Treat male partners who have been in contact with affected partners within 60 days of the onset of symptoms; make arrangements for treatment or facilitation of treatment.

In one case series, women with PID who cultured positive for Mycoplasma genitalium had an increased risk of short-term PID treatment failure with cefoxitin and doxycycline, resulting in high rates of sequelae (infertility [22%], recurrent PID [31%], and chronic pelvic pain [42%]).In patients who fail initial treatment, consider M.genitalium as a causative organism.
Percutaneous drainage or surgery may be required for definitive treatment of tubo-ovarian abscess.

Adolescents randomized to a video intervention at diagnosis of PID were significantly more likely to have their partners treated than those in the control group; there were no differences in medication completion, sexual abstinence, or partner notification.
Consider hospitalization for patients who fail 72 hours of outpatient therapy, who have tubo-ovarian abscess, or who are pregnant, or if other surgical emergencies cannot be excluded.
Also consider hospitalization if the patient is not capable of following or is unable to tolerate an outpatient regimen.
Hospitalize patients with severe illness including but not limited to high fever, nausea, uncontrollable vomiting, or pain.
Give doxycycline by mouth when possible to prevent pain with IV infusion.
Tubo-ovarian abscess is the most important complication.
About 1 in 8 women with PID experience difficulty with fertility, 30% have chronic pelvic pain, and 1% will later develop ectopic pregnancy. B
Offer all patients with PID an HIV test. C
Re-culture those with positive cervical cultures in 4 to 6 weeks. C
PID is associated with a high morbidity: 20% of women with PID experience infertility, 30% continue to report chronic pelvic pain, and 1% subsequently develop an ectopic pregnancy.
Multiple PID infections lead to a 4- to 6-fold increase in risk for permanent fallopian tube damage.
In a review of 7 studies, one demonstrated a significant association between chlamydia infection and ovarian cancer.
Offer all patients with PID an HIV test.
Re-evaluate patients with positive cervical cultures in 4 to 6 weeks.
Gonorrhea is a reportable disease; contact the local health department.
Treat male partners who have been in contact with affected partners within 60 days of the onset of symptoms; make arrangements for treatment or facilitation of treatment.
PID has a high morbidity; patient education on prevention is key.
Stress the importance of completing the course of treatment.

Screen pregnant women as early as possible for syphilis and chlamydia, and high-risk women for gonorrhea (age 25 and younger or from an area in which gonorrhea is common); perform initial or repeat testing for any symptoms in the third trimester to avoid infant infection.

Hospitalize and use parenteral treatment with the least teratogenic potential. Authors of a Cochrane review concluded that amoxicillin or erythromycin are acceptable alternative therapies for genital chlamydial infections in pregnancy, with clindamycin and azithromycin considered if these drugs are contra-indicated or not tolerated.

list.listitem: Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM Ceftriaxone 500 mg intramuscular (IM) IM single

Cefoxitin 2 g IM and probenecid 1 g orally AND doxycycline 100 mg orally twice a day for 14 days WITH metronidazole 500 mg orally twice a day for 14 days (covers bacterial vaginosis and anaerobes). Alternative: a third generation cephalosporin (e.g., ceftizoxime or cefotaxime) AND doxycycline 100 mg orally twice a day for 14 days WITH cefoxitin 2 g IM and probenecid 1 g orally AND doxycycline 100 mg orally twice a day for 14 days with or without metronidazole Cefoxitin 2 g IM and probenecid 1 g orally AND doxycycline 100 mg orally twice a day for 14 days WITH metronidazole 500 mg orally twice a day for 14 days (covers bacterial vaginosis and anaerobes) OR anaerobes) Alternative: athird

In cases of cephalosporin allergy, if community prevalence and risk-factors for GC are low and follow-up likely, consider use of fluoroquinolones for 14 days (levofloxacin 500 mg orally once daily, ofloxacin 400 mg twice daily, or moxifloxacin 400 mg orally once daily) with metronidazole for 14 days (500 mg orally twice daily).

Prior to initiating therapy, test for gonorrhea using culture; if the test is positive, treatment should be based on results of antimicrobial susceptibility. Consult with an infectious disease specialist if the isolate is quinolone resistant.

Preferred: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV OR cefotetan 2 g IV every 12 hours OR cefoxitin 2 g IV every 6 hours AND doxycycline 100 mg orally or IV every 12 hours WITH metronidazole 500 mg oral or IV every 12 hours (use with ceftriaxone regimen only) Preferred: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV OR cefotetan Preferred: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV OR cefotetan 2 g IV every 12 hours OR cefoxitin 2 g IV every 6 hours AND doxycycline 100 mg orally or IV every 12 hours WITH metronidazole 500m g oral or IV every 12 hours (use with ceftriaxone regimen only) Preferred: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV OR cefotetan
